title: From JSC engineering office to NASDAQ space prime
body:
## The man who rebuilt Columbia

Stephen Altemus joined NASA in 1989, starting at Kennedy Space Center before moving to Johnson Space Center in Houston, where he would spend the better part of a decade working in the Engineering Directorate's Aeroscience and Flight Mechanics Division. He had earned a Bachelor of Science in Aeronautical Engineering from Embry Riddle Aeronautical University and a Master's in Engineering Management from the University of Central Florida — a pedigree that placed him among the technicians who made NASA's human spaceflight program run. He was not yet the public face of anything.

On February 1, 2003, the Space Shuttle Columbia disintegrated during re-entry over Texas and Louisiana, killing all seven crew members. The loss triggered one of the most exhaustive accident investigations and physical reconstruction efforts in aerospace history. Altemus was assigned as Columbia Reconstruction Director — the engineer responsible for organising the recovery of debris across 2.3 million acres and leading the technical reconstruction that would help investigators determine what had failed. It was a role that required institutional discipline, the ability to manage hundreds of people under sustained public and political scrutiny, and a capacity to hold enormous operational complexity without flinching. It remains, in the language of aerospace, one of the most demanding engineering management assignments of the modern era.

He was subsequently appointed Director of Engineering at JSC, and later Deputy Director of the entire centre — the second-ranking operational position at the institution that manages human spaceflight for the United States government. When he left NASA in 2013 to co-found Intuitive Machines, he carried with him not only a technical record but a set of institutional relationships across the agency that very few private-sector executives could replicate.

## A thesis about what NASA would become

The founding thesis, in 2013, was structural rather than speculative. Altemus co-founded the company in Houston with Dr. Kamal Ghaffarian, a serial deep-tech entrepreneur whose career had already produced Stinger Ghaffarian Technologies — a technical services firm that KBR would acquire in 2018 — and would go on to include co-founding Axiom Space, X Energy, Quantum Space, and PTX. Ghaffarian brought the entrepreneurial architecture and the capital-formation relationships; Altemus brought the NASA institutional credibility and the engineering rigour. Together, they made a bet that NASA's exploration mandate was shifting from agency-owned execution toward commercial procurement — and that a Houston-based aerospace company with deep JSC roots could be the private partner of choice for lunar logistics and deep space.

The thesis took five years to receive its first institutional validation. In 2018, NASA selected Intuitive Machines as one of the initial participants in the Commercial Lunar Payload Services programme — the procurement vehicle through which the agency intended to buy lunar delivery as a service rather than build the capability itself. The CLPS award gave Intuitive Machines a formal channel for what it had been building toward. Through 2019 to 2023, the company developed the Nova-C lander platform, a vehicle class designed to deliver up to 100 kilograms of NASA and commercial payloads to the lunar surface. It was an era of engineering development on a very long timeline, funded by NASA milestones and private capital, without any of the quarterly reporting obligations that would soon arrive.

## The SPAC window and the public listing

In February 2023, Intuitive Machines completed its business combination with Inflection Point Acquisition Corp., the special-purpose acquisition company sponsored by Michael Blitzer's Inflection Point organisation. Blitzer was the founder of Kingstown Capital Management, a multi-billion-dollar asset manager, and had built Inflection Point as a SPAC vehicle specifically oriented toward technology and innovation businesses. He joined the board of Intuitive Machines concurrent with the de-SPAC, in the role that would eventually chair the Strategic Transactions Committee — the committee that would later approve the $800 million Lanteris acquisition.

The company began trading on NASDAQ under the ticker LUNR. The board that assembled alongside the listing reflected a deliberate configuration: Dr. Ghaffarian as Chairman (Class III), Altemus as CEO and director (Class III), William Liquori as a Class I director carrying the credential of a retired Lieutenant General and Chief Strategy and Resourcing Officer of the United States Space Force, and Robert Masson as Class I director and Audit Committee Chair — a Naval Aviator turned CFO whose career had run through Raytheon, Flowserve, and Hypertherm with a Harvard Business School MBA as its foundation. In June 2023, the company appointed Nicole Seligman — former President of Sony Entertainment, former EVP and Global General Counsel of Sony Corporation, a Harvard Law magna cum laude graduate who had clerked for Justice Thurgood Marshall and was then serving as an OpenAI board director — as a Class II director.

The board that emerged was, by any measure, overqualified for a company at that revenue scale. It was also precisely calibrated for what Intuitive Machines needed: deep national-security procurement relationships, aerospace-finance rigour, and corporate-governance depth sufficient to manage a company navigating the intersection of NASA contract law, public-market expectations, and a genuinely novel operating environment.

## Odysseus lands on the Moon

On February 15, 2024, a SpaceX Falcon 9 lifted the Nova-C IM-1 lander — named *Odysseus* — from Kennedy Space Center. Seven days later, on February 22, *Odysseus* touched down near the Malapert A crater at the lunar south pole, becoming the first privately-built spacecraft to successfully land on the Moon and the first US-built spacecraft to soft-land on the lunar surface since Apollo 17 in December 1972. It was the moment the founding thesis, eleven years after Altemus and Ghaffarian registered the company in Houston, received its clearest physical proof.

The landing came with operational complications. A failure of the landing legs caused *Odysseus* to come to rest on its side, partially obscuring the solar panels and compressing the mission timeline. The lander nonetheless transmitted data and demonstrated that commercial lunar landing was a viable, repeatable capability rather than a theoretical one. In the early months of 2025, the IM-2 mission — *Athena* — launched carrying additional NASA and commercial payloads, reached the lunar surface, and encountered similar operational difficulties. Two missions, two lunar landings, two sets of lessons about the genuine difficulty of precision surface operations at 384,000 kilometres.

## Building the executive team for scale

As *Odysseus* was completing its mission in early 2024, the company was also reshaping its executive team for the transition from development-stage operator to operating-scale contractor. In September 2024, Peter McGrath joined as Chief Financial Officer, stepping into the role from his position as Vice President of Business Development at Intuitive Machines. McGrath had spent 31 years at Boeing, across structural analysis, Phantom Works, and launch services — a career that gave him both the engineering economics literacy and the large-programme financial management experience that a company approaching $300 million in annual revenue and a $4.82 billion NASA contract ceiling required.

The CLPS ceiling expansion itself, completed through 2024 and 2025, was a significant signal. NASA raised the total contract ceiling to $4.82 billion, with $150 million in guaranteed near-term task orders across the programme. The $180.4 million IM-5 task order — the largest single CLPS award to date, directing seven science and technology payloads to the Lunar South Pole aboard the larger cargo-class Nova-D lander — confirmed that Intuitive Machines was not merely one of several CLPS participants but was emerging as the programme's primary operational contractor.

## The Lanteris transaction and the identity shift

The single most consequential event in the company's history arrived with the announcement of the $800 million acquisition of Lanteris Space Systems — $450 million in cash and $350 million in stock, with an expected close in the first quarter of 2026. Chris Johnson, who had served as CEO of Lanteris and before that as President of Boeing Satellite Systems International, was named President of Lanteris Space Systems within Intuitive Machines effective January 2026. The acquisition brought Boeing-grade satellite systems product lines into a company that had built its identity entirely around lunar delivery. Total backlog post-Lanteris rose to $943 million.

The executive realignment of February 2026 formalised the new structure: Dr. Timothy Crain, the co-founder who had engineered the Nova-C lander platform after a NASA JSC career that spanned Mars Science Lander navigation and Orion spacecraft guidance systems, became Senior Vice President and Chief Technology Officer. Anna Jones — a Northwestern Law JD whose career had run through Latham and Watkins, ConocoPhillips, Marathon Oil, and Paysafe — became Senior Vice President, Chief Legal Officer, and Corporate Secretary.

## What the arc means

At the frozen snapshot of May 23, 2026, Intuitive Machines had guided FY2026 revenue of $900 million to $1 billion — three to four times the FY2025 base — with positive Adjusted EBITDA. The shape of the company that Altemus and Ghaffarian founded in a Houston office in 2013, incorporated the credential of a man who rebuilt a destroyed Space Shuttle and the entrepreneurial capital of a serial deep-tech founder, is now something qualitatively different from what it was when *Odysseus* lifted off in February 2024.

The thirteen years from founding to a billion-dollar revenue outlook trace one of the more unusual arcs in the post-commercial-space era: a company that survived the SPAC cycle with its institutional credibility intact, executed two lunar landings before its competition reached the launchpad, and used the operational proof points from those missions to justify a transformational acquisition that repositions it as a full space prime. The Columbia Reconstruction Director credential that Altemus carried out of JSC in 2013 was never merely biographical colour. It was the institutional signal — to NASA, to the Pentagon, to the aerospace primes — that the people running Intuitive Machines had operated at the hardest end of the business before they ever asked anyone to trust them with a commercial lunar lander.
